title: Beyond Field-Line Descriptions: Electromagnetic Energy Transport in Intended Antennas
content: Antennas are conventionally described through time-varying currents and charges, standing-wave distributions, near and far electromagnetic fields, impedance, radiation resistance, and Poynting-vector energy transport. These formulations accurately predict antenna behavior, but they do not necessarily provide an intuitive structural account of how electromagnetic energy is organized along a conductor and subsequently released into surrounding space. This article develops a complementary physical interpretation of intended antenna operation within the Beyond Field-Line Descriptions framework. Conventional antenna and electromagnetic theory are retained as the quantitative foundation, while the proposed Photony interpretation treats the antenna as a spatially distributed electron-transduction system. Regions of relatively high current are associated predominantly with magnetic structuring through internal electrons, whereas regions of relatively high voltage are associated predominantly with electric structuring through surface-associated electrons. During each half-cycle, changing voltage and current conditions produce growth, reduction, reversal, and pinch-off of the corresponding electric and magnetic chains. The resulting structures are proposed to separate progressively from the transducing electron population and propagate outward as organized electromagnetic energy. Particular attention is given to the standing-wave distribution along a dipole antenna, the distinct timing of electric and magnetic pinch-off, the transition from source-coupled structuring to outward energy transport, and the relationship between the proposed chain interpretation and the conventional Poynting-vector description. The framework is intended as a structural interpretation of established antenna behavior rather than a replacement for conventional antenna equations.
